questions.q: Why does this case study's order-to-fulfillment business process decompose into three separate integration flows rather than one?
options: Because Salesforce requires every business process to use exactly three integrations
Because three flows is always the correct number for any order-management scenario
Because the WMS cannot support more than one integration at a time
Because each flow (order to WMS, status updates back, shipping-rate lookup) has different answers to the four framing questions, pointing toward different patterns for each
questions.explain: The three flows have genuinely different initiators, frequencies, volumes, and urgency levels, so each one points toward a different pattern — forcing them into a single uniform pattern would have made at least one of them a poor fit.

questions.q: Why does Flow 1 (order created in Salesforce, sent to the WMS) use an idempotency key based on the order's unique Salesforce ID?
options: To make the flow run faster
So that a retried publish after an ambiguous failure never risks the WMS picking and fulfilling the same order twice
Because idempotency keys are required by the REST API specification
To avoid needing an API version on the WMS's endpoint
questions.explain: The idempotency key lets the WMS recognize a retried publish of the same order as a duplicate of an already-handled request, directly applying Lesson 15's idempotency concept to prevent a duplicate fulfillment.

questions.q: Why does Flow 2 (fulfillment status updates flowing back from the WMS) use an event-driven, fire-and-forget pattern rather than synchronous communication?
options: Because status updates are too large in volume for synchronous calls
Because the WMS cannot make synchronous calls under any circumstances
Because a rep or customer checking order status doesn't need sub-second updates, and eventual consistency (a status update arriving a few seconds late) is an entirely acceptable trade-off here
Because fire-and-forget guarantees instant delivery, unlike synchronous calls
questions.explain: The urgency answer for status updates tolerates a short delay, making eventual consistency acceptable — exactly the condition under which Lesson 8's event-driven, fire-and-forget pattern is the right fit rather than a tightly coupled synchronous call.

questions.q: Why is Flow 3 (shipping-rate calculation at checkout) the one flow in this case study that justifies synchronous communication?
options: Because the rep is staring at a screen waiting for a number before they can proceed — a genuinely immediate need, unlike the other two flows
Because shipping rates never change and can be cached forever
Because synchronous communication is always required for any callout involving money
Because the shipping carrier's API only supports synchronous calls
questions.explain: Flow 3's urgency answer is genuinely immediate — the rep cannot proceed with the quote without the rate right now — which is exactly the condition Lesson 6 identifies as justifying synchronous communication despite its availability-coupling cost.

questions.q: What does this case study say would have gone wrong with a single-minded "everything must be asynchronous" instinct applied to all three flows?
options: Nothing; asynchronous patterns are always strictly better for every flow
It would have violated Salesforce's governor limits for all three flows
It would have made Flow 1 and Flow 2 more fragile against WMS downtime
Flow 3's rep would be left staring at a blank screen with no shipping cost and no way to proceed, since that flow genuinely needs an immediate synchronous answer
questions.explain: Forcing Flow 3 (the checkout rate lookup) into an asynchronous pattern would leave the rep with no way to complete the quote in the moment, since that specific flow's urgency answer genuinely requires a synchronous, immediate response.
